# **3.5 System Design and Development**

         This section details the engineering methodology used to transform the conceptual framework derived in Chapter II into a functional hardware-software prototype. Every design decision is described using the TRI (Topic, Restriction, Illustration) writing framework, where the Topic introduces the specific component or technology, the Restriction narrows it to the exact role and constraints within the TOMS project, and the Illustration provides the precise specifications, parameters, or configurations used.

1. ## **Requirements Analysis**

### **Functional Requirements**

         The functional requirements for the TOMS system were derived directly from the four research questions (RQ1–RQ4) and the research gaps identified in the systematic literature review (Chapter II). Each requirement addresses a specific deficiency of the traditional "konduktor" system in Iligan City.

         (T) The first requirement concerns the automated generation of a real-time, digital passenger manifest without relying on visual head counting. (R) For this specific project, the manifest is generated through a dual-triggering mechanism: the conductor physically docks a Slave terminal onto the Master handheld device via spring-loaded pogo pins, or the passenger presses a physical tactile button on the Slave terminal to initiate boarding. (I) Each boarding event is recorded as a structured binary payload containing a 32-bit UTC epoch timestamp, a 16-byte passenger identifier derived from the RFID card UID or the ESP32's hardware eFuse MAC address, a boarding type flag (card, button, or QR), the fare in centavos as a 16-bit unsigned integer, and the seat and route numbers as 8-bit unsigned integers.

         (T) The second requirement addresses the accurate calculation of fares and the issuance of a tamper-proof digital receipt to replace consumable paper tickets. (R) In this architecture, the Master device determines the fare based on a locally stored fare table containing the route identifier and the base fare in centavos, then transmits the computed amount to the Slave, which generates a QR code as the passenger's receipt. (I) The QR receipt encodes a plaintext string formatted as "TOMS|VEH_ID|TIMESTAMP|FARE|UID," rendered on a 128×160 pixel ST7735S TFT LCD using the LVGL 8.3 graphics library at a resolution suitable for scanning by standard smartphone cameras.

         (T) The third requirement mandates offline-first data storage, ensuring the system continues recording transactions even when the mobile phone and its internet connection are not attached. (R) For this design, the Master ESP32 stores all passenger events locally in a SPIFFS (SPI Flash File System) partition, with records buffered into binary log files of up to 1,000 records per file before rotating to a new file. (I) The SPIFFS partition is mounted at the path "/storage" with a dedicated partition label defined in the device's partition table configuration. Unsynced log files are identified by a ".log" extension; once successfully transferred to the phone, they are renamed to ".done" and eventually cleaned up to reclaim flash space.

         (T) The fourth requirement concerns secure, authenticated communication to prevent unauthorized boarding commands and protect transaction data from tampering. (R) In this implementation, anti-fraud security is achieved through a two-layer approach: a UID-based handshake at the physical UART level and AES-256-CBC payload encryption at the application level. (I) Every boarding command payload contains a 16-byte target UID field that must match the Slave's own eFuse MAC address, zero-padded to 16 bytes; if the UID does not match, the packet is silently dropped. The application-layer encryption is handled by the mbedTLS library compiled into the Espressif ESP-IDF framework, using a 256-bit AES key stored in Non-Volatile Storage (NVS).

         (T) The fifth requirement specifies a real-time phone dashboard that provides the transport operator with a live view of boarding activity and device health. (R) For this project, the dashboard is a native Android application built with the Flutter framework, connected to the Master ESP32 via USB On-The-Go (OTG). (I) Communication uses a TinyUSB CDC-ACM (Communications Device Class – Abstract Control Model) virtual serial port, exchanging newline-delimited JSON messages at 115,200 baud. The phone sends commands such as "handshake" and "get_status," and the Master responds with JSON events for each boarding event, device status updates including battery percentage and pending log count, and pogo-pin dock state changes.

### **Non-Functional Requirements**

         (T) The system must use commercially available, low-cost components suitable for small-scale transport operators. (R) This project exclusively uses Espressif ESP32-S3 microcontrollers, which retail for approximately ₱200–₱400 per unit, paired with an ST7735S TFT display module costing approximately ₱150. (I) The total bill of materials for one Master–Slave pair, excluding the Android phone, is estimated below ₱1,500, placing it well within reach of local cooperatives and individual operators.

         (T) The Master device must be handheld and battery-powered to accommodate the mobile nature of minibus operations. (R) For this design, the Master ESP32-S3 is powered by a single-cell lithium-polymer battery monitored via an Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) on a dedicated GPIO pin. (I) A firmware utility function reads the raw ADC value and converts it to millivolts using the ESP-IDF ADC calibration API, providing the battery percentage to the phone dashboard in real time.

         (T) The system must process a boarding event within a time frame acceptable for a moving vehicle. (R) In this implementation, the end-to-end latency from button press to QR display must not exceed five seconds. (I) The firmware achieves this by allocating dedicated FreeRTOS tasks pinned to specific CPU cores: the USB CDC task runs on Core 0 at priority 5 with a 4,096-byte stack, the ESP-NOW handler runs on Core 1 at priority 6 as a latency-sensitive task with a 4,096-byte stack, the UART sync task runs on Core 0 at priority 4 with a 4,096-byte stack, and the LVGL UI rendering task on the Slave runs with an 8,192-byte stack protected by a FreeRTOS mutex to guarantee thread-safe screen updates.

2. ## **Design**

         The design phase translates the requirements into a concrete hardware wiring plan, a communication protocol, a firmware task model, and a mobile application architecture. Each subsystem is described independently so that it may be tested, debugged, and replaced without affecting the others.

1. ### **System Architecture**

**Overall System Topology**

         (T) The TOMS architecture follows a three-tier topology comprising an embedded Slave terminal, an embedded Master handheld device, and a mobile phone application. (R) For this specific project, the topology is organized as a strict master-driven hierarchy: the Slave is a passive display-and-receipt device that never initiates business logic; the Master orchestrates all fare decisions and acts as the bridge between the physical hardware and the digital world; and the Flutter mobile application serves as the cloud gateway and operator dashboard. (I) The data flow proceeds unidirectionally in normal operation: a boarding trigger, whether a pogo-pin dock or a button press, causes the Slave to send its unique identifier to the Master. The Master validates the identifier, constructs a boarding command containing fare, seat, route, and vehicle information, and sends it back to the Slave. The Slave renders the fare screen and QR receipt, while the Master simultaneously logs the event to SPIFFS and forwards a JSON summary to the phone over USB CDC. The phone stores the event in a local SQLite database and, when internet connectivity is available, synchronizes the records to a Supabase cloud backend.

**Master Firmware Architecture (ESP32-S3)**

         (T) The Master firmware is built on the Espressif ESP-IDF 5.5.3 real-time operating system framework and is organized into six independent modules. (R) For this device, the ESP32-S3's dual-core Xtensa LX7 processor is exploited to separate latency-sensitive radio operations on Core 1 from I/O-bound USB and UART tasks on Core 0. (I) The six modules and their FreeRTOS task assignments are summarized in Table 3.1.

**Table 3.1.**  
*Master firmware module assignments and FreeRTOS task parameters*

| Module | Core | Priority | Stack Size | Function |
| :---- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---- |
| USB CDC | 0 | 5 | 4,096 B | TinyUSB CDC-ACM phone I/O using newline-delimited JSON protocol. |
| UART Sync | 0 | 4 | 4,096 B | Pogo-pin state machine (DISCONNECTED → DETECTING → SYNCING → CONNECTED → TRANSMITTING). UART1 at 115,200 baud on GPIO 2 (TX) and GPIO 3 (RX), with dock detect on GPIO 4. |
| ESP-NOW | 1 | 6 | 4,096 B | ESP-NOW 2.4 GHz radio for wireless Slave communication with a 1-second blocking event queue. |
| Storage | 0 | 3 | 2,048 B | SPIFFS log write and NVS configuration with periodic flush of buffered events. |
| Crypto | — | — | — | AES-256-CBC encryption via mbedTLS with the key loaded from NVS at boot. |
| Power | — | — | — | Battery ADC monitoring; exposes battery millivolts and percentage to the USB status response. |

         The initialization sequence in the main entry point proceeds through seven explicit steps: (1) Storage initialization including NVS and SPIFFS, (2) Crypto initialization loading the AES-256 key from NVS, (3) ESP-NOW initialization in Wi-Fi station mode without connecting to any access point, (4) USB CDC driver installation via TinyUSB, (5) UART Sync initialization including the UART1 driver and dock GPIO interrupt, (6) Power monitoring with ADC calibration, and finally (7) the creation of all four FreeRTOS tasks pinned to their respective cores.

**Communication Protocol**

         (T) All inter-device communication uses a single, unified packet format shared across both ESP-NOW (wireless) and UART (wired) channels. (R) For this system, the protocol is defined in a shared library that is compiled identically into both the Master and Slave firmware, eliminating the possibility of format mismatch between devices. (I) The on-wire packet layout consists of a 2-byte synchronization word (0xAA55), a 1-byte payload length field, a 1-byte message type field, a 1-byte sequence number, a variable-length payload of 0 to 240 bytes, and a 2-byte CRC-16-CCITT checksum. The fixed overhead is 7 bytes. The maximum payload of 240 bytes accommodates the largest structure, the boarding command at 40 bytes, with significant headroom for future extensions. Message types are categorized by direction and summarized in Table 3.2.

**Table 3.2.**  
*Communication protocol message type categories*

| Category | Type Range | Messages |
| :---- | :---: | :---- |
| Slave → Master | 0x01–0x0F | PASSENGER_BOARD (0x01), BUTTON_PRESS (0x02), UID_RESPONSE (0x03) |
| Master → Slave | 0x10–0x1F | FARE_TABLE_UPDATE (0x10), CONFIG_SYNC (0x11), BOARD_COMMAND (0x12), UID_REQUEST (0x13) |
| Acknowledgments | 0x20–0x2F | ACK_MASTER (0x20), ACK_SLAVE (0x21), NACK (0x2F) |
| Utility | 0xF0–0xFF | HEARTBEAT (0xF0), TIME_SYNC (0xF1) |

**UART Pogo-Pin Handshake State Machine**

         (T) The physical docking mechanism between the Master and Slave uses spring-loaded pogo pins that establish a UART serial connection. (R) For this design, the handshake follows a five-state finite state machine that automatically progresses from physical contact to authenticated data exchange without any manual intervention from the conductor. (I) The first state, DISCONNECTED, represents the idle condition where the dock detect pin (GPIO 4) reads LOW, and the task polls every 10 milliseconds. When the dock pin transitions to HIGH, the system enters the DETECTING state, where an 80-millisecond debounce timer is started to reject transient contact from vibration. Upon successful debounce, the state advances to SYNCING: the Master sends a UID_REQUEST packet and waits up to 1,000 milliseconds for a UID_RESPONSE from the Slave containing its 16-byte eFuse MAC unique identifier and assigned seat number. Once the UID is validated, the CONNECTED state is reached, and the Master constructs a boarding command embedding the fare (default ₱13.00, or 1,300 centavos), route identifier, 16-byte vehicle UUID, and epoch timestamp, and transmits it over UART. The final state, TRANSMITTING, represents the window during which the Master waits for a PASSENGER_BOARD response from the Slave confirming that the QR code was displayed. Upon receipt, the event is logged to SPIFFS and forwarded to the phone. If the dock pin returns to LOW at any point during this sequence, the state machine immediately resets to DISCONNECTED and sends a dock disconnection event to the phone via USB CDC.

**Slave Firmware Architecture (ESP32-S3)**

         (T) The Slave firmware is also built on ESP-IDF 5.5.3 and is responsible for a single function: displaying boarding information and generating QR receipts on command. (R) For this system, the Slave is designed as a strictly passive terminal—it never initiates fare logic, never calculates prices, and never stores transaction history. (I) The Slave firmware is organized into five modules. The Display Driver interfaces with an ST7735S SPI-connected TFT LCD at 128×160 pixels using SPI2_HOST, with the SPI bus configured on GPIO 11 (MOSI), GPIO 12 (SCLK), GPIO 10 (CS), GPIO 9 (DC), GPIO 14 (RST), and GPIO 13 (Backlight PWM). The UI Engine uses the LVGL 8.3 graphics library with a double-buffer rendering strategy, where all six screen states (Welcome, Processing, Fare, QR, Error, and Sleep) are defined as an enumeration, and a FreeRTOS mutex protects all LVGL API calls from concurrent access between the main logic task and the LVGL timer task. The display adopts a dark-mode palette with a background color of 0x101010, card containers at 0x2A2A2A, teal accent borders, and the Montserrat 14-point font. The QR Generator module produces QR codes from the plaintext receipt string using a software encoding library and renders the resulting matrix directly onto the LVGL canvas. The Button Input module connects a physical tactile button via GPIO interrupt with software debounce; a press triggers a BUTTON_PRESS packet sent to the Master over ESP-NOW to initiate the manual boarding flow. Finally, the Deep Sleep Manager blanks the display via a dedicated sleep screen function before entering deep sleep, with wake sources including the button GPIO and a configurable timer.

**Mobile Application Architecture (Flutter/Android)**

         (T) The Flutter mobile application serves as the cloud gateway and real-time operator dashboard for the TOMS system. (R) For this project, the application is built with Flutter SDK 3.9.x targeting Android only, using the Provider package for state management and SQLite via the sqflite package for offline-first local storage. (I) The application is organized into four layers. The USB Service layer manages the USB CDC-ACM connection lifecycle using the usb_serial package, setting the serial parameters to 115,200 baud, 8 data bits, 1 stop bit, and no parity. Incoming bytes are accumulated into a line-based parser that splits on the newline character (0x0A), and each complete JSON line is decoded and dispatched by event type: acknowledgment events update the device status model, passenger events create new log records in SQLite, dock events update the dock state indicator, and error events surface diagnostic messages to the UI. The service also maintains a 200-entry raw message log buffer with timestamps for the real-time debug console. The Database Service layer wraps a local SQLite database with a single passenger_logs table containing columns for auto-increment ID, timestamp, boarding type, fare in centavos, seat number, route identifier, passenger ID, and a synced flag. Aggregate queries provide today's total revenue and passenger count. The Application State layer is a central change notifier that wires USB events to the database and exposes computed properties, such as today's revenue formatted in Philippine Pesos, recent logs, and dock state, to the widget tree. A periodic timer requests device status from the Master every 10 seconds when connected. The Dashboard UI layer presents a premium dark-mode interface with a curated color palette, featuring a Master device status card displaying battery percentage, pending logs, and UART state; gradient-backed stat cards for today's revenue and passenger count; a scrollable transaction feed with per-row sync status icons; and a floating action button for USB connect and disconnect. A dedicated Debug Console screen, accessible via a terminal icon in the app bar, provides quick-command chips, a color-coded TX/RX log viewer, and a raw JSON command input bar.

         The Android manifest declares USB host hardware as a required feature and includes an intent filter for USB device attachment so that the application auto-launches when the ESP32 Master is connected via USB OTG. A device filter XML file restricts auto-detection to Espressif vendor identifiers.

**Data Flow Summary**

         The complete end-to-end data flow for a single boarding event proceeds through seven stages. First, the boarding is triggered when the passenger presses the button on the Slave or the conductor docks the Slave onto the Master via pogo pins. Second, the Slave transmits its eFuse MAC unique identifier to the Master, either via ESP-NOW for a button press or via UART for a pogo-pin dock. Third, the Master validates the UID, constructs a boarding command with fare, seat, route, vehicle ID, and timestamp, and sends it back to the Slave. Fourth, the Slave verifies the target UID field, displays the fare screen for three seconds, generates and displays the QR receipt for eight seconds, and then returns to the welcome screen. Fifth, the Slave sends a PASSENGER_BOARD event back to the Master, which logs the event to SPIFFS and forwards a JSON representation to the phone via USB CDC. Sixth, the Flutter application receives the JSON event, inserts a passenger log record into the local SQLite database with the synced flag set to zero, and updates the dashboard statistics in real time. Seventh, when internet connectivity becomes available, a sync service queries the database for unsynced records, pushes them to the Supabase cloud backend in batches, and marks them as synced.

# **3.6 Testing and Validation (Hardware Focus: Module & Power Testing)**

          (T) The first requirement of the system's testing phase involves verifying the physical and electrical integrity of the PN532 NFC transceiver's I2C communication interface. (R) For this implementation, the diagnostic tests are executed at a fast-mode clock frequency of 400 kHz on GPIO 2 (SDA) and GPIO 3 (SCL) for both Master and Slave platforms, verifying that the initialization routine successfully retrieves the device's firmware version. (I) The driver firmware performs this test in `pn532_init()` by transmitting a raw request frame to the I2C address 0x24 and parsing the response payload; a successful test is indicated when the IC field reads 0x07 (representing the PN532 chip) and the firmware version fields return a major version of 0x01 and a minor revision of 0x06, confirming stable bus connectivity.

          (T) The second hardware verification test focuses on measuring the response latency of the active-LOW interrupt IRQ line of the NFC transceiver. (R) In this design, the Master IRQ pin is mapped to GPIO 4 and the Slave IRQ pin is mapped to GPIO 5 (preserving GPIO 4 as the dedicated wake-up button), with both inputs configured as falling-edge triggers to eliminate the CPU overhead associated with continuous I2C register polling. (I) Using a digital storage oscilloscope, the latency from the moment an initiator card or target enters the RF field to the assertion of the IRQ line (transitioning from 3.3V to 0V) is measured; the test demonstrates that the system latency drops from a polling average of 250 milliseconds to an interrupt service routine response time of under 2 milliseconds, enabling immediate handshake establishment.

          (T) The third test validates the reliability and packet delivery rate of the NFC-DEP (ISO 18092) Peer-to-Peer communication link. (R) For this project, P2P transactions are tested exclusively at a baud rate of 424 kbps in passive mode, where the Master functions as the Initiator (calling `pn532_in_jump_for_dep` to retrieve the target's parameters) and the Slave functions as the Target (`pn532_tg_init_as_target` transmitting its 10-byte NFCID3 containing its hardware eFuse MAC address). (I) A specialized test suite executes 1,000 sequential boarding transactions, sending a compact 20-byte payload containing the fare index, seat assignment, and timestamp, and waiting for a 2-byte ACK response; the test achieves a packet success rate of 99.9% at a distance range of 0 to 2 centimeters, proving the robustness of the NFC link in high-vibration public utility environments.
